To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
DARPP‐32 is present in a subset of neurons in the primate cortex, and its distribution is developmentally regulated.

DARPP‐32 is expressed by neurons in layer V of the cortex in newborn monkeys and by neurons in layer Va in the adult, but not in the newborn; DARPP‐32 expression in layer V is developmentally related to the expression of D‐1 receptors, which are also found in layer V in the newborn but not in the adult; DARPP‐ 32 is expressed by a subpopulation of interstitial neurons in the newborn but is not found in this location in the adult;

DARPP‐32 is a phosphoprotein that is enriched in the dopaminoceptive cells bearing D‐1 dopamine receptors in the basal forebrain and that it is expressed in a large number of pyramidal neurons in the primate cortex.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the distribution and possible function of a phosphoprotein, DARPP‐ 32, in the cerebral cortex.
the development of the cerebral cortex in primates, with particular emphasis on the cellular and molecular events that occur after birth.
the distribution of DARPR‐32 in the rhesus monkey cerebral cortex and the relationship of this protein to the dopaminergic system and the dopamine D‐1 receptor.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the distribution of DAR PP‐32‐L IR neurons in the primate cortex is not uniform and is related to both the type of cortical area and the stage of development.

DARPP‐32 immunoreactivity in the primate cortex is found in pyramidal and nonpyramidal cells and in interstitial neurons, that the distribution of these cells is highly heterogeneous and that the distribution of DARP‐32‐positive neurons is not necessarily correlated with the distribution of D‐1 receptor‐positive cells in the primate neocortex.
DARPP‐32 is expressed in a subpopulation of cortical pyramidal cells in the rhesus monkey and that its distribution is developmentally regulated and is related to the distribution of D‐1 receptors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
DARPP‐32 is expressed in pyramidal neurons of the cortex, but only in a limited number of areas, and that the expression is developmentally regulated.
DARPP‐32 is a good marker for D‐1 receptor bearing neurons in the primate cortex, and that the distribution of DARP‐32‐Lir neurons changes during development.

DARPP‐32 is a marker of dopaminoceptive cells in the primate cortex, and the distribution of DAR‐32‐positive neurons in layers Va and VI may be related to the corticofugal projection of the cerebral cortex to the basal ganglia.
The main takeaway from our work is that
DARPP-32 is a phosphoprotein found in the basal ganglion and the cortex.
the distribution of DARP-32 positive cells is not uniform in primate cortex and that the distribution is different in the adult and in the neonate.
DARPP‐32 is a useful marker to visualize the distribution of D1 receptors in the primate neocortex.
